summary: Defines the profile link relation type, which lets a representation indicate that it follows one or more profiles. A profile does not change the meaning of the representation but tells clients about extra constraints, conventions or extensions. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A profile adds extra rules to a document without changing what the document is. The document keeps its media type, so a client that ignores the profile still reads it correctly. This RFC registers a link relation named profile that lets a server point at a profile by URI.

subtitle: How to label a representation with extra rules and conventions without inventing a new media type.

tldr.problem: A media type tells a client what kind of representation it is handling, but a server sometimes needs to add extra rules or conventions for one particular representation without inventing a whole new media type.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers a link relation type named profile, so a representation or an HTTP Link header can point at one or more profile URIs. A profile only adds semantics and MUST NOT change the meaning of the representation for a client that does not know the profile.
tldr.outcome: The relation is registered with IANA, so any format that supports typed links can carry it. Clients that know a profile can apply its extra rules, and clients that do not can still read the representation correctly.

today: RFC 6906 is an Informational RFC published in March 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and the profile link relation type it registers with IANA is still the reference for using profiles with media types.

sections.title: Why Profiles Exist
sections.content:
Every resource representation sent over a protocol such as SMTP or HTTP carries a media type label, such as text/html, so a client can tell at run time what kind of content it is handling. Sometimes a server wants to say more about one particular representation than the media type alone can say.

HTML 4 had a built-in way to do this: the profile attribute of the head element. That mechanism worked for HTML alone, and the RFC notes that HTML 5 appeared likely to drop it. RFC 6906 generalises the idea instead. It registers a profile link relation type under the rules of RFC 5988, so it can travel in any representation that supports typed links and in HTTP Link headers.

The podcast feed is the example the RFC opens with. A feed can carry extra fields describing audio and video, and a profile link lets a client recognise that the feed follows those extra conventions even when the feed currently holds no podcast entries at all.
sections.plainLanguage: A media type label says what kind of content a client is looking at. Sometimes the server needs to add extra detail about one document. This RFC defines a link named profile that carries that detail.

sections.title: What a Profile Is
sections.content:
A profile is extra semantics used to process a resource representation: constraints, conventions, extensions, or anything else that does not alter the basic media type semantics. The RFC sets one hard rule. A profile MUST NOT change the semantics of the representation when it is processed without profile knowledge, so that clients with and without knowledge of the profile can both use the same representation safely.

Profiles are identified by URI, and that URI works as an identifier in the same way an XML namespace URI does. The presence of a particular URI has to be enough for a client to assert that a representation conforms to that profile. Clients SHOULD therefore treat profile URIs as identifiers and not as links, though a profile MAY be defined so that its URI does identify retrievable profile description. For profiles that may meet unknown clients, the RFC recommends that profile maintainers make the URI dereferenceable and provide useful documentation there. The design and representation of such profile descriptions are outside the scope of this document.

Profiles can be combined: a single resource representation can conform to zero profiles or to any number of them. Depending on which profiles a client supports, the same representation linked to several profiles can be processed with different sets of processing rules.
sections.plainLanguage: A profile is a named set of extra rules for reading a document. It must not change what the document means for someone who does not know the profile. The profile is named by a URI, and that URI works as a label rather than something to fetch.

sections.title: Profiles Versus New Media Types
sections.content:
A media type defines both the semantics and the serialisation of a kind of content. Many media types have room for extension, so a specific instance can layer additional semantics on top. When it does, a profile is the right way to signal that the original processing model still applies and that an additional processing model can be used to extract more meaning. A new media type, by contrast, defines a complete set of processing rules and semantics instead of adding to an existing set.

The RFC draws the line with two examples. XHTML is a new media type rather than a profile of XML, because it introduces a complete new perspective on the underlying XML structures and exposing the raw XML is not useful to XHTML clients. hCard is a profile of (X)HTML, because it adds processing rules that let a client extract vCard contact information from a representation without changing any HTML processing rule or semantic.

For newly defined media types that may be used with profiles, the RFC recommends that they SHOULD define a media type parameter called profile and specify that the parameter follows the profile semantics of this document. That lets a client request a profile when it interacts with a server, for example by setting the HTTP Accept header. A representation using the parameter SHOULD still carry the value inside itself as a profile link, because the media type label of a representation can easily get lost when it is taken out of its conversational context. Because a representation can link to more than one profile, a media type defining such a parameter SHOULD define it as a whitespace-separated list of profile URIs.

Profile links convey information about the use of profiles for a media type, and if they are used within a media type they apply to the context that media type specifies. Profile links in the head element of an HTML document apply to the document as a whole. Profiles used in profile media type parameters, or in HTTP Link headers, extend to the scope of the protocol in which they are used.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding rules on top of a format is a profile. Replacing the format's meaning entirely is a new media type. The RFC recommends that media types also accept a profile parameter, so a client can ask for a specific profile.

sections.title: Registration of the profile Relation
sections.content:
The profile link relation type has been registered with IANA per Section 6.2.1 of RFC 5988. The registered description reads: identifying that a resource representation conforms to a certain profile, without affecting the non-profile semantics of the resource representation.

The registration notes record that profile URIs are primarily intended to be used as identifiers, and that clients SHOULD NOT indiscriminately access profile URIs. The link relation type is independent of the context in which it is used and does not constrain, in any way, the target of the linked URI. For the purposes of this specification the target URI does not even have to identify a dereferenceable resource, or use a dereferenceable URI scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA has registered the relation name profile. The registration says clients should treat the profile URI as a label and should not fetch it automatically.

sections.title: Example Profiles
sections.content:
The RFC lists profiles that already exist, plus one case it treats as hypothetical. Profiles have so far been mostly limited to HTML, because HTML is where the mechanism was built in.

The hCard profile uses http://microformats.org/profile/hcard as its defining URI. It is a mechanism for embedding vCard information in an HTML page using the mechanisms provided by microformats. It shows both halves of what a profile has to do: define a model-based extension of the media type, in this case vCard fields, and define the way that extension is represented in the media type, in this case microformats. The same vCard information represented through RDF in Attributes or through microdata would need different extraction rules, so those would be identified by different profiles.

The Dublin Core profile, http://dublincore.org/documents/2008/08/04/dc-html/, embeds Dublin Core metadata in an HTML page. Unlike hCard, which uses microformats as its foundation, Dublin Core defines its own embedding method, using HTML link elements. Dublin Core also allows links to be added as metadata, so its profile describes both extra data inside the representation and extra resources the representation can be linked to.

Podcasts extend feed formats with a substantial set of additional attributes, because podcast entries are time-based media such as audio and video. There is no profile URI for podcasts yet; the RFC notes that the current definition, maintained by Apple, could serve as one, or could be updated to include one. A generic feed reader can still follow a podcast feed, but a podcast-aware feed reader can extract the additional information and therefore offer more sophisticated services or a more sophisticated interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives three profiles. hCard puts vCard contact details in HTML. Dublin Core puts metadata in HTML. Podcast feeds add fields for audio and video. In each case the profile names extra rules without changing what the feed or page is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the profile relation type is not known to introduce any new security issues beyond those already discussed in RFC 5988 for the generic use of Web linking mechanisms. It adds no security analysis of its own beyond that reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC finds no new security problems with this link type. It points to the Web Linking RFC for the security rules that already apply to links.
